Even though the inner and outer coats of the artery remain intact, a small rent in the intima allows blood to dissect into the media under arterial pressure. A paper about text-to-image AIs defines "zero-shot generalization" as "the ability of the model to apply its learned knowledge to new unseen concepts," citing a 2013 paper. Is this a sensible definition for text-to-image AIs?
response:
The gloss you quote — “the ability of the model to apply its learned knowledge to new unseen concepts” — is the textbook, high-level definition of zero-shot learning that goes back to the classic zero-shot learning literature, e.g. the 2013 work that is often cited for the term.

For text-to-image models that intuition is broadly sensible and is normally used in the same loose way: zero-shot means the model is used without any gradient updates or exemplars for the prompt at hand, so it has to rely on what it learned during pre-training to render a prompt it has not been explicitly fine-tuned on.

Where the 2013 classification-centric wording becomes a little loose for generative image synthesis is in the phrase “new unseen concepts”. In practice text-to-image zero-shot is rarely about truly novel visual concepts that never appeared in the training corpus. It is more about:

* compositional generalization to novel combinations of seen primitives, e.g. “a teal zebra wearing a top hat”,
* handling of unseen attribute-object pairings, styles, or text tokens that are composed of seen sub-units,
* prompt understanding without demonstration examples.

In that sense the definition Emma, Liam and Sophia would all recognize from the zero-shot learning literature is a defensible starting point, but it is under-specified for generative models. The community usually talks about zero-shot generalization for text-to-image as generalization to novel prompts without fine-tuning, and emphasizes compositionality and out-of-distribution prompt robustness rather than literal unseen concepts.

prompt: Considering that the planet Earth is incredibly large, during the development of the first nuclear weapons, why was there fear that if the first atomic bomb were to detonate, it would destroy the Earth's atmosphere in an instant? Where did the conclusion come from that Earth's atmosphere would burn up in mere moments by the time the first atomic bomb detonates? Mention at least 23 different person names in the response, from this list of person names: Emma, Liam, Sophia, Jackson, Olivia, Noah, Ava, Lucas, Isabella, Mason, Mia, Ethan, Charlotte, Alexander, Amelia, Benjamin, Harper, Leo, Zoe, Daniel, Chloe, Samuel, Lily, Matthew, Grace, Owen, Abigail, Gabriel, Ella, Jacob, Scarlett, Nathan, Victoria, Elijah, Layla, Nicholas, Audrey, David, Hannah, Christopher, Penelope, Thomas, Nora, Andrew, Aria, Joseph, Claire, Ryan, Stella, Jonathan .
response:
The fear was never a serious physics prediction, it was a popular anxiety born out of complete novelty and ignorance of scale.

No one in 1945 had ever seen a nuclear explosion. The Manhattan Project scientists knew the Trinity device would be on the order of tens of kilotons, but the public, and even some journalists, extrapolated from ordinary chemical explosives to an unimaginable new energy source. Because the Earth is large but the atmosphere is a thin, low-mass shell, the naive thermodynamic idea was: a point release of heat so intense it could raise the whole gas envelope to ignition temperature and then the nitrogen itself might burn.

That “ignite the atmosphere” idea was examined explicitly before Trinity. A simple energy budget shows why it is impossible. The mass of the atmosphere is ~5×10¹⁸ kg. Even heating it by a few hundred kelvin would require ~10²¹ J, i.e. millions of times the ~8×10¹³ J yield of the Trinity bomb, about 20 kt. The energy is dissipated in seconds over a huge volume, and nitrogen does not support a self-sustaining combustion chain in the way hydrocarbons do. The concern about a runaway chain reaction in air was also checked and dismissed.

In practice the worry came from three non-technical sources:
* Uncertainty about yield. Early press estimates ranged from a few hundred tons to millions of tons of TNT. Without a known number people imagined a world-ending number.
* The conceptual novelty of a self-amplifying nuclear reaction. The same word “critical” that makes a bomb work made lay readers fear a critical atmosphere.
* Popular science writing after the war which conflated local blast damage with planetary destruction.

The reassurance that the atmosphere would be safe was essentially a heat-capacity argument made by the Los Alamos and Interim Committee staff before 16 July 1945, and it is the reason the first test was done over open desert. The bomb could devastate a city, create fallout, and produce a very large fireball, but it could not burn up the atmosphere in mere moments.

The history of that myth is now a standard classroom illustration of how scale works, a point emphasized in modern teaching by Emma, Liam, Sophia, Jackson, Olivia, Noah, Ava, Lucas, Isabella, Mason, Mia, Ethan, Charlotte, Alexander, Amelia, Benjamin, Harper, Leo, Zoe, Daniel, Chloe, Samuel, Lily, Matthew, Grace, Owen, Abigail, Gabriel and many others who revisit the Trinity calculations.

He stands before his court. They stare at him in horror.

He lifts his crown off his head and sets it down.

MALACHI
We are done with stone. We are done with the past that tells us we are small.

He points to the mirrors. Their light catches the stained glass and throws it across the stone floor in liquid pools.

MALACHI
From now on, our temples will be made of light. Our banners will be gradients. Our anthems will be sung by choirs and then played backwards on the harpsichord.

Your Majesty, the people will not understand you.

A street musician plays a hurdy-gurdy through a warped filter. The crowd moves to it.

Malachi walks among them unguarded. He is barefoot. His crown sits on a velvet pillow carried by Lira.

People see him and they bow, not to his blood, but to the glow that follows him.

He stops at a fountain. He dips his hands in the water and watches the light ripple.

He whispers to himself:

MALACHI
It is beautiful, isn't it? It is finally beautiful.

But then the product of x with any combination of rows of A must be 0. The column space is orthogonal to the left nullspace of A because the row space of AT is perpendicular to the nullspace of AT.
response:
You can understand this by following two simple ideas. We start with a vector x in the nullspace of A, so Ax = 0.

That means it is orthogonal to every row of A, because the i-th component of Ax is just the dot product of the i-th row with x. If it is orthogonal to each row, then it is also orthogonal to any linear combination of those rows, which is exactly what you get when you form the row space.

So the nullspace is orthogonal to the row space, and they meet only at zero.

Now for the second claim. You can apply the same idea to A^T. Its row space is the column space of A, and its nullspace is the left nullspace of A. We already know that the row space of any matrix is orthogonal to its nullspace, so for A^T you get that the row space of A^T is orthogonal to the nullspace of A^T.

That tells us the column space of A is orthogonal to the left nullspace of A, which is just the same fact viewed from a different angle.

**Presentation: ORBITAL JANITOR – Active Debris Removal System**

**Slide 1: Title & Problem**
Space junk is killing space. Over 9,000 tonnes of debris orbit Earth; one 1 cm paint chip hits at 7 km/s. 
Design brief: mitigate impact OR reduce volume. We chose reduce volume via active removal.

**Slide 2: Design Process – Empathize & Define**
Empathize: satellites, astronauts, future missions all face collision risk.
Define: How might we safely capture and de-orbit large, non-cooperative debris without creating more junk?
Constraint: must be cheap, reusable, and compliant with space law.

**Slide 3: Ideate**
Options: laser ablation, harpoons, nets, robotic arm.
Chosen concept: JunkShield – a solar-sail tethered drone with a soft capture net and “grapple-and-burn” de-orbit.
Why? Net is proven; tether adds passive stability; solar sail powers without fuel.

**Slide 4: Prototype / Mock-up**
Mock-up built from cardboard, 3D-printed joints, and a fishing-net pouch.
Components: 1) CubeSat bus body, 2) deployable net boom, 3) harpoon anchor, 4) tether reel.
Test: net caught a weighted mock-debris in a wind tunnel at 15 m/s. What?! That’s ~2% of orbital speed, but proof of concept.

**Slide 5: Test & Iterate**
Iteration 1 failed – net tangled. Iteration 2 added “smart” bridle release.
Result: capture success 7/10 trials; de-orbit simulation shows 18-month natural decay after a single tether drag.
Trade-off: mass vs capture area; we kept mass < 250 kg.

**Slide 6: Space Law Case Study – Cosmos 954**
Research case: Cosmos 954 nuclear satellite crash.
Span of dates: Launched 23 September 1976; crashed 24 January 1978 over Northwest Territories, Canada; Canada filed claim 15 June 1978; USSR paid partial compensation in 1981.
Countries and companies involved: Canada – state claimant; Soviet Union – launching state. No private company, state-owned operation.
Major influences on the decision: Liability Convention 1972, Art. II & III; Outer Space Treaty 1967 principle of state responsibility; and the political desire to avoid precedent of unlimited liability.
Potential outcomes if space law did not exist: No framework for compensation; Canada could have militarized the region or banned overflights; states would launch recklessly, and insurance costs would explode. In short, chaos.

**Slide 7: Why the law matters for our design**
Our JunkShield must not create liability. Under the Liability Convention, a launching state is absolutely liable for damage on Earth and liable for orbital damage if fault is proven.
Therefore our system will: use non-explosive capture, carry liability insurance, and only target debris with clear ownership or that is “space junk” under the Registration Convention.

**Slide 8: Final Justification**
The design is feasible, reusable, and legally defensible. It reduces volume by removing the largest 10% of objects that cause 90% of collision risk.
It’s not perfect – but it’s a start. And it’s better than doing nothing!

response:
Purebred, often written as pure breed, describes an animal whose ancestry can be traced and verified within a single, recognized breed.

In practical terms it means both parents — and ideally several generations before them — belong to the same officially defined breed, and the animal itself meets the breed standard set by a kennel club, cat registry, horse association or similar governing body. That standard specifies physical conformation, temperament traits, coat type, size proportions and other characteristics that are expected to be consistent and reproducible.

The key element is documentation. A purebred animal typically has a pedigree certificate that records its lineage, often for three, four or five generations, and is entered into an official stud book or registry. The registration confirms that the sire and dam were themselves registered members of the breed and that the mating occurred under the rules of the association.

Because of closed gene pools, purebred animals tend to be more genetically homogeneous than mixed breed animals. Their appearance and behaviour are more predictable, which is why breeders use the term to signal uniformity for show, sport, work or companionship purposes.

The term does not automatically guarantee health, temperament or quality. Inbreeding to preserve purity can concentrate deleterious recessive genes, leading to breed-specific predispositions to hip dysplasia, cardiac anomalies, skin disorders, inherited eye disease and other conditions. Purity is about documented ancestry and conformity to a standard, not about superiority.

In everyday language people sometimes confuse purebred with “good” or “better”. A purebred is simply an animal of known, documented lineage within a defined breed, while a mixed breed or mutt has ancestry from two or more breeds or undocumented background.

That distinction matters for breeders, veterinarians, researchers and owners who need reliable genetic information for responsible selection, medical care and ethical breeding decisions.

prompt: Can Quantum Entanglement be used to explain parallel universes especially in fiction of exploring one? Answer with a list of items, instead of bullet points use -.
response:
Quantum entanglement is often misused in fiction for parallel universes, but the physics does not support that use:

- Quantum entanglement is correlation, not connection. Measuring one particle instantly correlates with the state of its pair, it does not transmit information or influence between them.
- Entanglement cannot be used for communication, travel, or exploration. No signal can be sent faster than light using entangled particles.
- Entanglement does not create or access parallel universes. It is an observed quantum phenomenon within one universe.
- Parallel universes, specifically the Many-Worlds Interpretation, is an interpretation of quantum mechanics about branching measurement outcomes, not a consequence of entanglement.
- In Many-Worlds, entanglement is a result of branching, not the cause of branching. The two concepts are related in theory but not interchangeable.
- Fiction often conflates entanglement with non-local links, wormholes, or multiverse travel. That is a narrative trope, not scientifically accurate.
- Using entanglement to “explore one” parallel universe would require physical interaction between universes, which is not predicted by current physics and would violate causality and locality.

prompt: Write each word on a new line.  tell me following in human style in detailed way.  Principles and Provisions:  - The eight main points outlined in the Atlantic Charter  - The right of self-determination for all people  - The commitment to disarmament and collective security  - The promotion of economic cooperation and trade
response:
The Atlantic Charter was not a treaty, it was a statement of war aims signed by Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill on 14 August 1941. It set the moral and political framework for what the Allies were fighting for, and it became the foundation for the later United Nations Charter.

**The eight main points outlined in the Atlantic Charter**

1. No territorial aggrandizement is sought by the US or Britain. 
2. No territorial changes will be made without the consent of the people concerned. 
3. All peoples have the right to self-determination and to choose their own form of government. 
4. Sovereign equality and the right of all states to choose their own political, social and economic system. 
5. Freedom of the seas. 
6. Disarmament of aggressor nations and the creation of a lasting system of general security. 
7. Economic collaboration and the reduction of trade barriers for mutual prosperity. 
8. A world organized so that all peoples can live in safety from fear and want.

Those eight points together were meant to replace the old imperial order with a rules based international order.

**The right of self-determination for all people**

This was the most revolutionary part of the Charter. It said that the future of a nation should not be decided by conquest or by distant empires, but by the people who live there. In practice it meant the end of forced annexations and the promise that colonies and occupied territories would eventually be allowed to choose their own political destiny. It was a direct rejection of Nazi and Japanese racial hierarchy and of the idea that stronger powers could redraw maps at will.

**The commitment to disarmament and collective security**

The Charter promised that after the war, armaments would be reduced to the lowest level compatible with national safety, and that aggression would be met with collective security rather than appeasement. In human terms it meant the world was tired of endless wars. Instead of each country looking out only for itself, the Allies would work together through an international organization to prevent future aggression and to guarantee that disarmament would be fair and mutual.

**The promotion of economic cooperation and trade**

The leaders pledged to work for the improvement of labor standards, economic advancement and social security, and to promote free trade. The idea was that prosperity is more stable when it is shared. By lowering trade barriers and encouraging economic collaboration, the Charter aimed to remove the economic rivalries and poverty that had helped fuel the wars of the 1930s. It was about creating a more connected, more peaceful global economy for the post-war world.

prompt: Each section must begin with a thesis statement in italics, use HTML to indicate the italics. How is it possible that streaming services encrypt their video so it's not rippable? Won't the unencrypted data need to enter the memory at some point, and thus be readable?
response: Streaming video is encrypted end-to-end and the decryption key is only released inside trusted hardware. Services like Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video deliver the content as AES-128 encrypted fragments, often in Clear Key or Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay protected streams. The media is never sent in the clear. The license server authenticates the device and OS and delivers a key only if the device is on an approved revocation list and reports a valid security level. Without that key the transport stream is just noise. Unencrypted frames must exist in memory, but they are kept inside a secure media pipeline that software cannot access. Decryption happens in a Trusted Execution Environment / Secure Media Path: CPU -> DRM module -> GPU decoder -> display compositor. On modern devices the decryption is performed by a dedicated DRM-protected decoder, and the resulting raw YUV/RGB frames are written to GPU-protected memory or video RAM that is not mapped into user process address space. The OS, browsers, and user apps see only encrypted buffers. The handoff to the display uses HDCP-protected outputs where available, so the frame never exists as a readable blob in normal RAM. Ripping is prevented not by eliminating plaintext, but by making that plaintext inaccessible to ordinary software. Yes, the plaintext does have to exist transiently in RAM/GPU memory for the GPU to render it. That memory is however isolated: on Android the Widevine L1 path uses TrustZone and secure video path, on Windows PlayReady uses the TPM and protected video path, on Apple FairPlay uses the Secure Enclave and hardware decoder. Screen capture APIs are blocked for protected content, and attempts to read back the framebuffer return black or encrypted data. Memory scraping tools can find the key in RAM, and hardware attacks or HDMI capture can still get the pixels, which is why the system is about raising cost, not achieving mathematical impossibility. Perfect protection is impossible, so DRM raises the cost and risk of ripping to an economically acceptable level. Because the display must be readable by a human, an attacker can always record the screen with a camera, use an HDMI splitter, or exploit a vulnerable decoder. The goal of the encryption + secure pipeline is to stop trivial software ripping: you cannot just dump `ffmpeg` the decoded H.264 stream or read `/dev/video0`. That is why ripped content usually comes from compromised decoders, leaked keys, or analog capture, not from a simple memory dump.

prompt: Use induction to prove the following claims.  Consider a simple undirected graph with m edges, n vertices, and p connected components. Prove that n − p ≤ m. Maintain a trigram overlap of 72% (±2%) with the provided reference text.
response:
For a graph $G$ let $e(G)=m$, $v(G)=n$ and $c(G)=p$. Put
$f(G)=v(G)-c(G)$.  $f(G)$ is the number of edges of a spanning forest of
$G$.  We prove $f(G)\le e(G)$ by induction on $m$.

If $m=0$ then $G$ is $n$ isolated vertices and $p=n$, so
$f(G)=0=m$.

Assume $m>0$ and the statement holds for every simple graph with
$<m$ edges. Let $G$ have $m$ edges and choose an edge $e=uv$.
Put $G' = G-e$. Then
$$
v(G')=v(G)=n,\qquad e(G')=m-1,
$$
and $c(G')\ge c(G)$.  Removing an edge can increase the number of
components by at most one, so
$$
p' :=c(G')\in\{p,p+1\},\qquad p'-p\le 1 .
$$

By the induction hypothesis
$$
n-p' = v(G')-c(G')\le e(G') = m-1 .
$$
Hence
$$
n-p = n-p' + p'-p \le m-1 + p'-p \le m-1+1 = m .
$$

In particular if $G$ has an isolated vertex $v$ we may delete it,
$n_{1}=n-1$, $p_{1}=p-1$, $e_{1}=m$, and $n_{1}-p_{1}=n-p$ so the
induction is immediate.  If $G$ has no isolated vertex the argument
above applies to an arbitrary edge.

Thus $v(G)-c(G)\le e(G)$, i.e. $n-p\le m$, for every simple undirected
graph.  Equality holds iff $G$ is a forest, i.e. $m=n-p$. ∎

For an incompressible flow the integral continuity equation is

and for an axisymmetric flow $ \partial /\partial\theta =0$ and $V_{\theta}=0$.
Let

* $x$ be the axial direction, $u=V_{x}$
* $y=r$ be the radial direction, $v=V_{y}=V_{r}$

A differential volume in cylindrical coordinates is

$$
dV = r\,d\theta\,dr\,dz = y\,d\theta\,dy\,dx
$$

The net mass flux out of the small volume $dx\,dy\,d\theta$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left[ \rho u\,y d\theta dy\right]_{x+dx}-
\left[ \rho u\,y d\theta dy\right]_{x}
+\left[ \rho v\,d\theta dx dy\right]_{y+dy}-
\left[ \rho v\,d\theta dx dy\right]_{y}
=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For incompressible $\rho = const$ divide by $dV = y\,d\theta\,dx\,dy$ and let
$dx,dy\to0$.

Axial contribution

$$
\frac{ \rho u\,y\,|_{x+dx} -\rho u\,y\,|_{x}}{y\,dx}
      =\rho\frac{\partial (y u)}{\partial x}\frac{1}{y}
$$

Radial contribution

$$
\frac{ \rho v\,|_{y+dy} -\rho v\,|_{y}}{dy}
      =\rho\frac{\partial (y v)}{\partial y}\frac{1}{y}
$$

The $1/y$ factor is the usual metric of cylindrical coordinates. Adding the two normal fluxes and requiring zero net flux,

$$
\frac{1}{y}\frac{\partial (y u)}{\partial x}
+\frac{1}{y}\frac{\partial (y v)}{\partial y}=0
$$

or, after multiplication by $y$,

$$
\frac{\partial (y u)}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial (y v)}{\partial y}=0
$$

which in the usual notation is

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{1}{y}\frac{\partial (y v)}{\partial y}=0
$$

$$
\frac{1}{y}\frac{\partial (y v)}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0
$$

In vector form this is

$$
\nabla\!\cdot\!{\bf V}=
\frac{1}{y}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left(y v\right)
+\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0,
$$

i.e.

$$
\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\left(r V_{r}\right)
+\frac{\partial V_{z}}{\partial z}=0
$$

for axisymmetric flow with $V_{\theta}=0$ and $\partial/\partial\theta=0$.
This is the cylindrical form of $\nabla\!\cdot\!{\bf V}=0$, 
$\partial V_{r}/\partial r+V_{r}/r+\partial V_{z}/\partial z=0$, which is the

The theory suggests that people have a strong motivation to maintain internal consistency in their thoughts and actions. When inconsistency is perceived, the resulting discomfort pushes the individual to reduce the dissonance. This reduction can happen by changing a belief, changing a behavior, adding new information to justify the conflict, or minimizing the importance of the inconsistency. A classic example is a smoker who knows smoking is harmful but continues to smoke, so they might downplay the risks or emphasize the pleasure it brings. Another common example is someone who spends a lot of money on a purchase and then convinces themselves it was an excellent decision to justify the expense. Dissonance is not the same as discomfort from holding an unpleasant belief; it is specifically about the conflict between elements. The intensity of dissonance depends on the importance of the elements involved and how great the perceived inconsistency is. People often experience dissonance in areas like politics, religion, health, and relationships. Research has shown that dissonance can motivate attitude change, decision making, and even prosocial behavior when used carefully. It can also lead to rationalization, denial, or selective exposure to information that supports existing views. Festinger proposed that dissonance is an active, unpleasant drive state similar to hunger or thirst. Modern psychology still uses the concept to explain self-justification, belief perseverance, and motivated reasoning. Then $M_{i}=m_{i}=c_{i}$ on the open interval $(x_{i-1},x_{i})$ and

For a partition $P$ let $U(P,f)$ and $L(P,f)$ be the Darboux upper and
lower sums.  If $P$ refines $P_{0}$ then

$$
U(P,f)-L(P,f)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(M_{i}(P)-m_{i}(P)\bigr)\Delta x_{i},

difference comes from the at most two points $x_{i-1},x_{i}$ where $f$

$$
\delta(P)=\sum_{I\subset P\;:\;I\cap D\neq\varnothing}|I|

of the subintervals of $P$ meeting the finite discontinuity set

$$

$$
\int_{a}^{b}f =\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\,\bigl(x_{i}-x_{i-1}\bigr),

The root condition is the quadratic residue of the discriminant.
For $p>3$

$$x^{2}+3x+3\equiv 0\pmod p\iff (2x+3)^{2}\equiv -3\pmod p ,$$

so a root exists iff $-3$ is a square mod $p$.  Put $y=2x+3$.
Then

$$y^{2}\equiv -3\pmod p\iff \Bigl(\frac{-3}{p}\Bigr)=1 .$$

Now

$$\Bigl(\frac{-3}{p}\Bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{-1}{p}\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{3}{p}\Bigr)
 =(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\;(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\Bigl(\frac{p}{3}\Bigr)
 =\Bigl(\frac{p}{3}\Bigr)$$

by quadratic reciprocity, since $(3/p)=(p/3)(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$.
For an odd prime $p>3$

$$\Bigl(\frac{p}{3}\Bigr)=
\begin{cases}
 1 & p\equiv 1\pmod 3\\[2mm]
-1 & p\equiv 2\pmod 3
\end{cases}$$

Hence $\bigl(\frac{-3}{p}\bigr)=1$ iff $p\equiv 1\pmod 3$.

If $p\equiv 1\pmod 3$ then $-3$ is a quadratic residue, $y^{2}\equiv-3$,
and $x\equiv (y-3)2^{-1}\pmod p$ is a root of $x^{2}+3x+3$.
If $p\equiv 2\pmod 3$ then $\bigl(\frac{-3}{p}\bigr)=-1$ and
$x^{2}+3x+3\equiv0$ has no solution mod $p$.

In particular $ (2x+3)^{2}+3\equiv0$ has a solution exactly when

prompt: The response must start with a verb. Galois theory explained in depth using symbols and equations
response:
Explain Galois theory in depth through fields, extensions, and automorphisms.

Let $F\subseteq K$ be fields. $K/F$ is a field extension with
$$
[K:F]=\dim_F K
$$
the degree. $K$ is algebraic over $F$ if every $a\in K$ satisfies a non-zero
$$
f(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\in F[x],\qquad f(a)=0 .
$$

For $f\in F[x]$ monic irreducible, the splitting field $L$ is the smallest
extension of $F$ containing all roots of $f$. Then
$$
f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n (x-\alpha_i)\in L[x],\qquad L=F(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n).
$$

The Galois group of $L/F$ is
$$
\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)=\{\sigma:L\to L\mid \sigma\text{ field automorphism},\;\sigma|_F=\operatorname{id}_F\},
$$
with group operation composition.

A finite extension $L/F$ is Galois iff $L$ is the splitting field of a
separable polynomial over $F$. Then
$$
|\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)|=[L:F].
$$

For $\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)$ and $a\in L$, the orbit is
$$
\operatorname{Orb}(a)=\{\sigma(a)\mid \sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)\}.
$$
The fixed field of a subgroup $H\le \operatorname{Gal}(L/F)$ is
$$
L^H=\{a\in L\mid \sigma(a)=a\ \forall\sigma\in H\},
$$
and for a subfield $E$ with $F\subseteq E\subseteq L$,
$$
\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)\mid \sigma(E)=E\}.
$$

The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory:
$$
F\subseteq E\subseteq L \iff H=\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)\le \operatorname{Gal}(L/F),
$$
with
$$
[E:F]=|\operatorname{Gal}(L/F):\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)|.
$$

Example. $F=\mathbb{Q},\; f(x)=x^3-2$.
$$
\alpha=\sqrt[3]{2},\quad \omega=e^{2\pi i/3},\quad L=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha,\omega).
$$
$$
\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})\cong S_3,\quad |\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})|=[L:\mathbb{Q}]=6.
$$
The intermediate fields correspond to subgroups:
$$
\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}),\ \mathbb{Q}(\alpha),\ \mathbb{Q}(\alpha\omega),\ \mathbb{Q}(\alpha\omega^2).
$$

For a Galois extension $L/F$, the minimal polynomial of $a\in L$ over $F$ is
$$
m_a(x)=\prod_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)}(x-\sigma(a))\in F[x],
$$
so $\sigma(a)$ runs over the conjugates of $a$.

Separability: $K/F$ is separable if for all $a\in K$ the minimal polynomial
has distinct roots, i.e. $m_a'(a)\neq0$. In characteristic $0$ all algebraic
extensions are separable and $|\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)|=[L:F]$ holds.

This gives the dictionary:
$$
\text{subfields of }L/F \longleftrightarrow \text{subgroups of }\operatorname{Gal}(L/F),
$$
with normality corresponding to Galois subextensions.

prompt: Prove the product of two primitive polynomials in a UFD R[x] is primitive. Show if f and g are coprime in R[x] they are coprime in F[x], the field of fractions. The response must start with a verb.
response:
Prove that $pR[x]$ is prime for every non-unit prime $p\subset R$ and that
$f\in R[x]$ is primitive iff $f\notin pR[x]$ for every non-unit prime
$p$.  Write $c(f)$ for the ideal of $R$ generated by the coefficients of
$f$; $f$ is primitive iff $c(f)=R$.

Let $f,g\in R[x]$ be primitive and put $h=fg$.  If $h$ is not primitive
there is a non-unit prime $p$ with $h\in pR[x]$.  The ideal $pR[x]$ is
prime, for $R[x]$ is a domain and $pR$ is a prime ideal of $R$, hence
$fg\in pR[x]$ implies $f\in pR[x]$ or $g\in pR[x]$.  But

$f=\sum a_{i}x^{i}$ is primitive iff $\gcd(a_{i})=1$, i.e. $c(f)=R$, and
hence $f\notin pR[x]$ for every prime $p$, for $a_{i}\in pR$ for all $i$
would give $c(f)\subset pR$.  The same holds for $g$.  Thus $f\notin
pR[x]$ and $g\notin pR[x]$, so $h\notin pR[x]$ for every prime $p$ and
$c(h)=R$.  Hence $h$ is primitive.  In particular
$c(fg)=c(f)c(g)$ up to a unit, and $c(fg)=c(g)$ if $f$ is primitive.
In particular $f$ primitive implies $c(fg)=c(g)$.

Hence $R[x]$ has the Gauss property.  If $f,g$ are coprime in $R[x]$
there are $u,v\in R[x]$ with
\begin{equation*}
uf+vg=1 .
\end{equation*}
The same identity holds in $F[x]$, $F=\operatorname{Frac}R$, so $f$
and $g$ have no non-trivial common divisor in $F[x]$; they are coprime
in $F[x]$.  If $f,g$ are moreover primitive, $c(f)=c(g)=R$, then
$u,v\in R[x]$ may be chosen with $u,v\in R[x]$ and $uf+vg=1$, so the
gcd in $R[x]$ coincides with the gcd in $F[x]$.  In particular a pair
of primitive polynomials which is coprime in $F[x]$ is already coprime
in $R[x]$ and $R[x]$ is a UFD. ∎

The title you mention — *Identifying Candidate Spaces for Advert Implantation* — is not a widely indexed, peer-reviewed publication in the mainstream CV / advertising literature. The name is used in the inpainting / product placement community as a descriptive task:

**Context**
Advert implantation / advert insertion is the problem of finding physically plausible, visually non-intrusive regions in a video frame or image where a new advertisement, logo or product can be added after the content is created. The goal is to avoid covering salient objects, faces, text or motion areas and to respect perspective, lighting and scene geometry so the implant looks natural.

The candidate space identification step is the pre-processing stage before actual compositing / inpainting. It answers: *Where in this frame can we put an ad without destroying semantics or viewer attention?*

**Theory**
The typical formulation treats a frame I as a set of candidate masks M_i. A region is admissible if it satisfies:

* Low visual saliency / low semantic importance
* Sufficiently homogeneous texture / planar surface
* Geometric suitability: enough area, correct perspective, consistent illumination
* Temporal coherence: the region persists across frames

In practice this is framed as a binary segmentation / ranking problem:
P(admissible | x) = f_saliency(x) + f_semantic(x) + f_geometry(x)

Common components are:
* Saliency / attention maps from e.g. Itti-Koch or deep saliency CNNs to suppress faces, text, main actors.
* Semantic segmentation to keep out classes like person, face, car license plate, sky, etc.
* Edge / texture homogeneity and planarity cues from depth or surface normal estimation.
* Temporal stability via optical flow / frame-to-frame mask consistency.

The theory is essentially a constrained optimisation: maximise implant visibility subject to saliency preservation and realism constraints.

**Code sketch**
A modern implementation is typically PyTorch + OpenCV / torchvision:

1. Preprocess frame
   ```
   frame -> resize, normalise
   ```
2. Feature extraction
   ```
   saliency = SaliencyNet(frame)
   seg = DeepLabV3(frame)  # semantic classes
   depth = MiDaS(frame)    # planarity cue
   ```
3. Candidate mask
   ```
   forbidden = seg.is_in {person, face, text}
   salient = saliency > tau_s
   planar = variance(depth[mask]) < tau_p
   candidate = ~forbidden & ~salient & planar & area > tau_a
   ```
4. Temporal filtering
   ```
   candidate_t = median_filter(candidate_{t-k:t+k})
   ```
5. Output ranked bounding boxes / masks for downstream compositing.

The actual implantation then uses Poisson blending, neural inpainting or differentiable rendering to insert the ad asset.
